screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives frame the skills you'll build when working with basic read operations in MongoDB. First, you will execute queries using the find method to retrieve documents from a collection. That means you'll write predicates that select records by field values or ranges and run them in the shell or via a driver. Second, you will apply comparison operators like greater-than, less-than, and membership operators to filter data precisely. You will practice $gt, $lt, $gte, $lte, $eq, $ne, $in, and $nin to express numeric, string, and set-based conditions. Third, you'll learn to combine multiple clauses using logical operators such as $and, $or, $not, and $nor so you can express compound business rules. We will explain the difference between implicit $and and explicit logical forms. Fourth, you will control returned fields with projection and manage result sets using limit, skip, and sort for pagination and sorted displays. Each objective ties to practical examples against a bookstore or products collection so you can practice and verify results.

screens.title: find() and Query Predicates
screens.narratorSegment: The heart of reading data in MongoDB is the find operation. At its simplest, find with no arguments returns a cursor for every document in a collection, but in practice you nearly always pass a query predicate — a document that describes the conditions a document must meet to be returned. A predicate uses fields as keys and either direct values for implicit equality or operator expressions for comparisons. For example, specifying name: "Alice Smith" is an implicit equality match. A predicate can be as simple as one field or a compound document combining several fields and operators. It's important to remember that find returns a cursor object. In an interactive shell it prints results for convenience, but application drivers require you to iterate or convert the cursor. As a concrete example, if you want to get all products with price greater than 100 you would use the predicate that compares the price field with the greater-than operator. A common misconception is thinking the predicate is S Q L-like where clauses always act the same; MongoDB predicates are documents and support nesting, arrays, and operator expressions that are expressive and composable. Your takeaway: predicates are JSON-like documents that describe the filter; practice writing them against a sample collection to build fluency.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A query predicate is a document passed to find() that expresses which documents to match; it can be simple equality or use operators for richer filters.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › find() & Predicates
What is a predicate?

A predicate is a JSON-like document passed to find() that defines selection rules. Use direct field:value for equality or operator sub-documents for comparisons and membership tests.

Implicit equality
Example: find documents where name equals a specific string.
Comparison operators
Use $gt, $lt, and others to express numeric and date ranges.
Cursor note
find() returns a cursor which you must iterate in application code; mongosh prints the first results automatically.
Key Takeaway
Treat the predicate as the primary tool for narrowing results; test predicates in the shell before using them in production code.
Example and visual
db.products.find({ price: { $gt: 100 } })
Concrete example
Find products priced above 100 to create a premium product list or pricing report.
Common mistake
Expecting find() to return an array in drivers; you must iterate the cursor or convert it to a list explicitly.
Pro tip
Test predicates with small datasets and explain() before deploying to production to check performance implications.
Check your understanding
Write a predicate to find books where inStock is true and publicationYear greater than 2018.

screens.title: Comparison Operators
screens.narratorSegment: Comparison operators let you move beyond simple equality checks to express ranges and membership. The default behavior of specifying field: value is equivalent to an $eq operator. Use $gt and $lt for greater-than and less-than comparisons, and $gte or $lte when you need inclusive bounds. For sets of allowed values use $in to match any of the listed values and $nin to exclude them. These operators are placed as a sub-document for the field you are testing. For example, price: { $gt: 100 } selects documents with a price greater than 100. A typical use-case is filtering products by price bands or genres by membership; $in is perfect when a product can belong to multiple acceptable categories. A common misconception is to chain operators for the same field as separate top-level conditions; when you need multiple operators on the same field, put them together in a single sub-document or use $and with explicit clauses. Also be careful with type mismatches: comparisons operate on stored types, so numbers stored as strings will not behave like numbers. Practice building filters for price and stock ranges and use explain() if performance becomes a concern.

keyIdea.title: Comparison summary
keyIdea.text: Use comparison operators to express ranges and membership; combine properly when multiple operators apply to the same field.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Comparison Operators
Operators list
  • $eq — equality (also default when no operator used).
  • $ne — not equal.
  • $gt / $lt — greater than / less than.
  • $gte / $lte — inclusive bounds.
  • $in / $nin — membership or exclusion from a list of values.
Example
db.products.find({ price: { $gt: 100 } })
db.products.find({ category: { $in: ["Electronics","Peripherals"] } })
Practical notes
Same-field combinations
Place multiple operators inside one field sub-document or use $and when necessary for clarity or repeated field conditions.
Type awareness
Comparisons use stored types. Numbers stored as strings will not compare numerically. Validate schema or normalize types before filtering.
Common mistake
Attempting to mix inclusion and exclusion operators for the same field incorrectly. Follow the rules for projections and for operators, group them properly.
Check
Try a query to find books priced between 20 and 40 using $gte and $lte and project title and price only.

screens.title: $in and $nin: Matching Sets of Values
screens.narratorSegment: Matching against sets of allowed or disallowed values is common when categories or tags matter. MongoDB's $in operator checks whether a field's value is any one of the specified values, while $nin ensures it is not any of them. These operators are useful when you want to return documents belonging to any of a small set of categories — for example, products in Electronics or Peripherals. They also work well for enumerated fields like status codes or genre lists. When the field stores an array, $in matches if any array element matches one of the values in your $in list. A subtle misconception is assuming $in performs a deep array comparison; it only tests elements, not structural equality. Another practical note: $in with a very large array can be inefficient; prefer a different design if you frequently test membership against very large sets. Use $nin to filter out specific values, which can be handy when excluding discontinued categories. As an example, find all products in either of two categories with one concise predicate. Practice these operators against the bookstore to filter multiple genres at once.

keyIdea.title: Membership matching
keyIdea.text: $in selects documents whose field equals any value in a list; $nin excludes those values. Useful for category membership and array element matching.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › $in / $nin
Examples
db.products.find({ category: { $in: ["Electronics", "Peripherals"] } })

db.products.find({ category: { $nin: ["Discontinued", "Obsolete"] } })
Note
If the field stores an array, $in checks for any matching element. Avoid huge lists inside $in for performance reasons.
Practical cards
Use-case
Filter product lists for multiple allowed categories in a single request for display or reporting.
Common mistake
Passing a huge array to $in; this can be slow and memory-intensive during query planning. Consider tagging strategies or precomputed indices.
Pro tip
When excluding a small number of known bad values, $nin is concise; for complex exclusions consider structuring data to make exclusion simpler.

screens.title: Logical Operators: $and, $or, $not, $nor
screens.narratorSegment: Logical operators let you combine multiple conditions into a single predicate. MongoDB implicitly applies an AND when you list multiple fields at the top level of the query document — every condition must be true. Use $and explicitly when you need to apply multiple conditions to the same field or when clarity helps. The $or operator returns documents where at least one clause is true and is essential for alternative business rules, such as products that are either expensive in one category or low-stock in another. $not inverts an expression, often used to negate a single operator, and $nor applies a NOR logic, returning documents where none of the listed conditions are true. A practical example combines $or with inner conditions to express branch logic: either category is Electronics and price above a threshold, or category is Peripherals and stock below some value. A common pitfall is misreading implicit AND behavior and attempting to mix contradictory conditions for the same field without grouping. Practice transforming complex English rules into a combination of implicit AND, $or arrays, or explicit $and clauses. The clearer your logical structure, the easier it will be to reason about correctness and performance.

keyIdea.title: Logical composition
keyIdea.text: Use implicit AND for simple multi-field conditions; apply $or, $and, $not, and $nor to express alternatives and negations precisely.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Logical Operators
Examples
db.products.find({ category: "Electronics", stock: { $gt: 50 } })

// explicit $and
db.products.find({ $and: [ { category: "Electronics" }, { stock: { $gt: 50 } } ] })

// $or with mixed clauses
db.products.find({ $or: [ { category: "Electronics", price: { $gt: 1000 } }, { category: "Peripherals", stock: { $lt: 100 } } ] })
Notes and pitfalls
Implicit AND: top-level multiple fields act as an AND; this is concise and common.
Same-field operators: use a single sub-document or $and to apply multiple operators to one field.
$not vs $ne: $not inverts an expression and can be used with operators; $ne is a direct not-equal check.
Check your logic
Translate an if-else rule into $or and nested predicate clauses and verify results in the shell.

screens.title: Projection: Return Only the Fields You Need
screens.narratorSegment: Projection controls which fields a query returns. The second argument to find() is a projection document where you set fields to 1 to include or 0 to exclude them. For example, when building a product list you might return only name and price to keep payloads small. The _id field is included by default; if you don't want it, set _id to 0. Important rule: you cannot mix include and exclude in the same projection document, with the one exception of _id. That means you either list fields to include or fields to exclude, not both. A typical example projects title and price while excluding the internal _id field. Projection also helps avoid over-fetching nested objects or large binary fields. A common beginner mistake is relying on projection to enforce security; projection reduces what is returned but does not affect authorization. Also be mindful that projecting computed values or slices requires aggregation or projection operators; simple inclusion/exclusion is best for performance and clarity. Practice projecting in the shell and examine the returned documents to ensure only intended fields are present.

keyIdea.title: Projection rules
keyIdea.text: Use projection to include (1) or exclude (0) fields; do not mix inclusion and exclusion except for _id, which you can explicitly exclude if needed.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Projection
Basic projection syntax
db.products.find({}, { name: 1, price: 1, _id: 0 })

// include only name and price, exclude _id
Rule: include OR exclude, not both (except _id).
Why: mixing confuses intent and can cause errors; the server expects one mode for efficiency.
Cards
Performance benefit
Reducing returned fields saves network and client processing, especially for large documents.
Security note
Projection reduces what is returned but is not a substitute for access control; always secure data at the application and database level.
Try this
Project author and title only from books and confirm _id is excluded by adding _id: 0.

screens.title: Cursor Methods: sort(), limit(), skip()
screens.narratorSegment: Once you have a predicate and projection, use cursor methods to control the result set. sort orders documents by fields; pass 1 for ascending and -1 for descending. limit restricts how many documents are returned and is useful for top-N queries or page sizes. skip offsets the cursor by discarding the first n documents, often used together with limit to implement simple pagination. For example, to get the three cheapest products you'd sort by price ascending and limit to three. A common pitfall is using skip for deep pagination: the server still scans and discards skipped documents, which can be slow for large offsets. For deep paging, prefer range-based paging on an indexed field or use a bookmark token. Also remember that the order of chained cursor methods matters for readability: apply sort then skip then limit in a predictable sequence. In application code you may need to materialize the cursor into an array or stream it depending on driver APIs. Practice combining projection with sort and limit to build paginated product lists that remain responsive and efficient. Cursor Methods: sort(), limit(), skip() means use sort to order results, limit to restrict size, and skip to offset pages; avoid deep pagination with skip in large datasets.. In practical terms, order, size, and offset your query results for ui and pagination. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Cursor Methods
Chaining example
db.products.find({}, { name: 1, price: 1, _id: 0 })
  .sort({ price: 1 })
  .limit(3)
Order tips: sort before limit to control which documents are considered for the top N.
Pagination: combine skip and limit for simple pages, but avoid skip for deep offsets.
Cards
Three cheapest products
Sort by price ascending and limit to 3 to display top cheap items.
Skip caution
Using skip with large values causes scanning overhead; consider range queries on an indexed field for better performance.
Try this
Retrieve titles of the 5 oldest books by sorting publicationYear ascending and limiting to 5.

screens.title: Cursor Behavior: Shell vs Drivers
screens.narratorSegment: A key operational detail to keep in mind: find() returns a cursor, not a complete array of documents. In the interactive shell, mongosh will iterate and display the first set of results for convenience, often hiding the cursor semantics. In application code, drivers return the cursor object so the application can iterate, stream, or transform results as needed. This distinction affects memory and performance: materializing an entire cursor into memory may be fine for small result sets but dangerous for large ones. Drivers provide APIs to iterate asynchronously, stream documents, or convert a limited portion into an array. When writing server-side code, explicitly control how many documents you fetch at once and combine projection and limit to reduce load. Another brief pitfall: assuming shell pagination equals driver pagination. Always test the behavior in the environment you'll run queries in. Practice writing small driver-style loops or using cursor methods to retrieve a known, limited number of documents so your code handles results predictably. Cursor Behavior: Shell vs Drivers means find() produces a cursor; mongosh auto-iterates some results for convenience, but drivers require explicit iteration or streaming of results.. In practical terms, understand that find() returns a cursor and how that differs across environments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Performance and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: Query correctness is only half the story; query performance and safety matter equally. Complex or unindexed queries on large collections can be slow because MongoDB may need to scan documents or index entries. Always test queries with explain() to view the execution plan. If you observe collection scans or large index bounds, consider adding appropriate indexes in a later module. Another safety issue is deep pagination: skip can become costly because the server still processes and discards skipped documents. For large datasets prefer range queries on an indexed field such as a timestamp or _id for efficient pagination. Also be careful to avoid returning unnecessary large fields like binary blobs or long arrays; use projection to prevent excessive network transfer. Finally, validate input in application code to avoid injecting incorrect types into predicates, which can yield unexpected results. These safety and performance steps will make your read operations reliable and fast when the dataset grows. Performance and Safety Notes means use explain() to inspect query plans, avoid unindexed scans, and prefer range-based paging for large result sets instead of deep skip.. In practical terms, test queries, watch for missing indexes, and prefer safe pagination patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the essential ideas to keep front of mind. First, find() with a query predicate is the primary read operation; predicates are JSON-like documents that express which documents to return. Second, comparison operators like $gt, $lt, $gte, $lte, $eq, $ne, $in, and $nin let you express ranges and memberships precisely. Third, logical operators including implicit AND, $and, $or, $not, and $nor allow you to build compound selection rules. Fourth, projection controls which fields are returned; include fields with 1 or exclude with 0 but do not mix inclusion and exclusion except for the special _id behavior. Fifth, find() returns a cursor; mongosh provides convenient printing, while drivers require iteration. Sixth, cursor methods sort, limit, and skip let you order and size results, but skip is costly for deep pagination. Keep testing queries with explain() and prefer range-based paging on indexed fields for scale. These core concepts combine to form reliable, efficient read operations in MongoDB.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to retrieve documents from MongoDB using the find method and the query language that powers it. We start with the basic idea that find returns a cursor of matching documents and then explore how a query predicate filters those documents with comparison and logical operators. You'll see how projection reduces the fields returned, and how cursor methods like sort, limit, and skip shape the final result. Practical examples use a products or bookstore collection so the concepts map directly to real queries you will run in the shell or from application code. We also highlight common beginner mistakes: assuming find returns a plain array, mixing inclusion and exclusion in projection, and overusing skip for deep pagination. By the end of this chapter you will be able to craft targeted queries, return only the fields you need, and paginate or sort results with confidence. Keep an eye out for performance notes — inefficient queries on large collections can be slow and will be addressed throughout.

These four objectives frame the skills you'll build when working with basic read operations in MongoDB. First, you will execute queries using the find method to retrieve documents from a collection. That means you'll write predicates that select records by field values or ranges and run them in the shell or via a driver. Second, you will apply comparison operators like greater-than, less-than, and membership operators to filter data precisely. You will practice $gt, $lt, $gte, $lte, $eq, $ne, $in, and $nin to express numeric, string, and set-based conditions. Third, you'll learn to combine multiple clauses using logical operators such as $and, $or, $not, and $nor so you can express compound business rules. We will explain the difference between implicit $and and explicit logical forms. Fourth, you will control returned fields with projection and manage result sets using limit, skip, and sort for pagination and sorted displays. Each objective ties to practical examples against a bookstore or products collection so you can practice and verify results.

Beyond the raw syntax, these objectives map to the tasks you'll perform in applications. Executing precise find queries lets you implement search pages, admin filters, and A P I endpoints that return just the right records. Mastering comparison and logical operators helps you convert business rules like price ranges, inventory thresholds, or combined category conditions into efficient queries. Projection is often overlooked, but returning only necessary fields speeds responses and lowers memory use on clients. Cursor controls — sort, limit, skip — are essential when building paginated lists or leaderboards. You will also learn to spot common pitfalls: relying on mongosh's automatic cursor printing instead of iterating in drivers, and using skip for deep pagination without planning for performance. Each micro-skill includes a small practice prompt using the bookstoreDB so you can run, inspect, and iterate on queries immediately.

The heart of reading data in MongoDB is the find operation. At its simplest, find with no arguments returns a cursor for every document in a collection, but in practice you nearly always pass a query predicate — a document that describes the conditions a document must meet to be returned. A predicate uses fields as keys and either direct values for implicit equality or operator expressions for comparisons. For example, specifying name: "Alice Smith" is an implicit equality match. A predicate can be as simple as one field or a compound document combining several fields and operators. It's important to remember that find returns a cursor object. In an interactive shell it prints results for convenience, but application drivers require you to iterate or convert the cursor. As a concrete example, if you want to get all products with price greater than 100 you would use the predicate that compares the price field with the greater-than operator. A common misconception is thinking the predicate is S Q L-like where clauses always act the same; MongoDB predicates are documents and support nesting, arrays, and operator expressions that are expressive and composable. Your takeaway: predicates are JSON-like documents that describe the filter; practice writing them against a sample collection to build fluency.

Comparison operators let you move beyond simple equality checks to express ranges and membership. The default behavior of specifying field: value is equivalent to an $eq operator. Use $gt and $lt for greater-than and less-than comparisons, and $gte or $lte when you need inclusive bounds. For sets of allowed values use $in to match any of the listed values and $nin to exclude them. These operators are placed as a sub-document for the field you are testing. For example, price: { $gt: 100 } selects documents with a price greater than 100. A typical use-case is filtering products by price bands or genres by membership; $in is perfect when a product can belong to multiple acceptable categories. A common misconception is to chain operators for the same field as separate top-level conditions; when you need multiple operators on the same field, put them together in a single sub-document or use $and with explicit clauses. Also be careful with type mismatches: comparisons operate on stored types, so numbers stored as strings will not behave like numbers. Practice building filters for price and stock ranges and use explain() if performance becomes a concern.

Matching against sets of allowed or disallowed values is common when categories or tags matter. MongoDB's $in operator checks whether a field's value is any one of the specified values, while $nin ensures it is not any of them. These operators are useful when you want to return documents belonging to any of a small set of categories — for example, products in Electronics or Peripherals. They also work well for enumerated fields like status codes or genre lists. When the field stores an array, $in matches if any array element matches one of the values in your $in list. A subtle misconception is assuming $in performs a deep array comparison; it only tests elements, not structural equality. Another practical note: $in with a very large array can be inefficient; prefer a different design if you frequently test membership against very large sets. Use $nin to filter out specific values, which can be handy when excluding discontinued categories. As an example, find all products in either of two categories with one concise predicate. Practice these operators against the bookstore to filter multiple genres at once.

Logical operators let you combine multiple conditions into a single predicate. MongoDB implicitly applies an AND when you list multiple fields at the top level of the query document — every condition must be true. Use $and explicitly when you need to apply multiple conditions to the same field or when clarity helps. The $or operator returns documents where at least one clause is true and is essential for alternative business rules, such as products that are either expensive in one category or low-stock in another. $not inverts an expression, often used to negate a single operator, and $nor applies a NOR logic, returning documents where none of the listed conditions are true. A practical example combines $or with inner conditions to express branch logic: either category is Electronics and price above a threshold, or category is Peripherals and stock below some value. A common pitfall is misreading implicit AND behavior and attempting to mix contradictory conditions for the same field without grouping. Practice transforming complex English rules into a combination of implicit AND, $or arrays, or explicit $and clauses. The clearer your logical structure, the easier it will be to reason about correctness and performance.

Projection controls which fields a query returns. The second argument to find() is a projection document where you set fields to 1 to include or 0 to exclude them. For example, when building a product list you might return only name and price to keep payloads small. The _id field is included by default; if you don't want it, set _id to 0. Important rule: you cannot mix include and exclude in the same projection document, with the one exception of _id. That means you either list fields to include or fields to exclude, not both. A typical example projects title and price while excluding the internal _id field. Projection also helps avoid over-fetching nested objects or large binary fields. A common beginner mistake is relying on projection to enforce security; projection reduces what is returned but does not affect authorization. Also be mindful that projecting computed values or slices requires aggregation or projection operators; simple inclusion/exclusion is best for performance and clarity. Practice projecting in the shell and examine the returned documents to ensure only intended fields are present.

Once you have a predicate and projection, use cursor methods to control the result set. sort orders documents by fields; pass 1 for ascending and -1 for descending. limit restricts how many documents are returned and is useful for top-N queries or page sizes. skip offsets the cursor by discarding the first n documents, often used together with limit to implement simple pagination. For example, to get the three cheapest products you'd sort by price ascending and limit to three. A common pitfall is using skip for deep pagination: the server still scans and discards skipped documents, which can be slow for large offsets. For deep paging, prefer range-based paging on an indexed field or use a bookmark token. Also remember that the order of chained cursor methods matters for readability: apply sort then skip then limit in a predictable sequence. In application code you may need to materialize the cursor into an array or stream it depending on driver APIs. Practice combining projection with sort and limit to build paginated product lists that remain responsive and efficient. Cursor Methods: sort(), limit(), skip() means use sort to order results, limit to restrict size, and skip to offset pages; avoid deep pagination with skip in large datasets.. In practical terms, order, size, and offset your query results for ui and pagination. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Close this chapter with three compact ideas you should be able to explain to a teammate. First, a query predicate is a document passed to find() — it defines selection rules using field keys and operator expressions. Second, projection and cursor methods shape what and how many fields are returned; use projection to trim payloads and sort/limit/skip to order and page results. Third, performance matters: test queries with explain(), avoid deep skip for large offsets, and be mindful of missing or inappropriate indexes. These three ideas — correctness of predicates, control of returned data, and attention to performance — are enough to build reliable read operations in most applications.
